Following Section 2.3 of Discrete Mathematics, an Open Introduction.Let \(\{a_n\}\) be a sequence of real numbers. The \(k^{th}\) forward difference of this sequence are defined recursively:
The first forward difference \(\Delta a_n\) is an new sequence defined by:\(\Delta a_n=a_{n+1}-a_{n}\).
The \(k\)th forward difference \(\Delta^{k} a_n\) is \(\Delta^{k} a_n=\Delta^{k-1} a_{n+1}- \Delta^{k-1}a_{n}\). So if the sequence for \(a_n\) is \(1,3,5,7,9, \ldots\) then \(\Delta a_n\) is \(3-1,5-3,7-5,9-7, \ldots= 2,2,2,2,2, \ldots\).




Find \(\Delta\) and \(\Delta^2\) for the following sequences :

\(2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, \ldots\)
\(1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, \ldots\)




Make up sequences that have:

3, 3, 3, 3, … as its second differences.
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, … as its third differences.
1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … as its fifth differences.




Find the closed form solution to the sequence using the using the polynomial fitting method for the sequence \(0, 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, 48, 63, 80,\ldots\) which has the recurrence \(a_n = a_{n-1} + 2n+1\) with \(a_0=0\).



Find the closed form solution to the sequence using the using the polynomial fitting method for the sequence \(1, 4, 10, 20, 35, 56, 84,\ldots\) which has the recurrence \(a_n = 4a_{n-1} - 6a_{n-2} + 4a_{n-3} - a_{n-4}\) with \(a_1=1, a_2=4, a_3=10\) and \(a_4=20\). This also happens to the be the sequence given by summing up the triangular numbers. That is, \(a_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T_n\).



Calculate \(\Delta \binom{n}{4}\). Use this to rewrite \(\Delta \binom{n}{k}\) as a binomial coefficient.






Prove \(\Delta (\Delta^i a_n)=\Delta^{i+1} a_n\).



Let \(b_n=n^3\). Prove \(\Delta^2 b_n=6n+6\).



\(\bigstar\) Let \(b_n=n^k\). Prove \(\Delta b_n=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\binom{k}{i}n^{i}\)



\(\bigstar\) Let \(a_n=\alpha^n\) for \(n \ge 0\) and \(\alpha\) a real number. Prove \(\Delta^k a_n=(\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha})^k a_n\) for all \(k \ge 0\).



\(\bigstar\) Let \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) be sequences. Prove \(\Delta (a_n\cdot b_n)=a_{n+1}\Delta b_n + b_{n}\Delta a_n\).

Discrete math is a fun departure from the calculus series, free from concerns about continuity and the real numbers. We get our first chance to explore abstract structures and a first introduction to proofs in this course. Discrete math ultimately boils down to counting, something that is tangible, comfortable, and sometimes even comforting.



Prerequisite: MATH 230
Topics include: Sets, algebraic systems, axioms, definitions, propositions, and proofs. Combinatorics, graph theory, moduli calculus. Coding, coding errors, and Hammang codes. Students are expected to write mathematical proofs, and communicate mathematical ideas clearly in written and oral form.

title: Direct Proofs
text:
Directions: Attempt to prove as many of the following problem as you can using the direct proof method.
Problem 1: Show \(\binom{2n}{2}=2\binom{n}{2}+n^2\)
Problem 2: Show \(\binom{n}{1} ^2=\binom{n}{2}+ \binom{n+1}{2}\)
Problem 3: Show \(\binom{n}{0}+\binom{n+1}{1}+\binom{n+2}{2} =\binom{n+3}{2}\) (Hint: Is there another way to write \(\binom{n}{0}\) to make the calculation easier?)
Problem 4: Show \(\binom{n}{k}\binom{n-k}{l}=\binom{n}{l}\binom{n-l}{k}\) with \(k+l \leq n\).
Problem 5: Let \(n\) be a positive integer. Show that \(\binom{2n}{n+1}+\binom{2n}{n}=\frac{1}{2}\binom{2n+2}{n+1}\)
Problem 6: If \(n\) an odd integer, then \(n^2\) is odd.
Problem 7: Let \(n\) any integer, then \(n^3-n\) is even.
Problem 8: Let \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) be integers. If \(a\) divides \(b\), and \(b\) divides \(c\), then \(a\) divides \(c\).
Problem 9: Let \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) be integers. If \(a^2+b^2=c^2\) is even, then at least one of the integers \(a\) and \(b\) is even.

title: Counting with Reccursion
text:
Definitions
The order of a recursive formula is the number of preceding values that are needed to calculate the next value. For example, the Fibonnacci recursion has order 2, and the Triangular number recursion has order 1.
A recurrence is called linear if it has the form \[a_n=c_1\cdot a_{n-1}+c_2\cdot a_{n-2} \cdots + c_k\cdot a_{n-k} +f(n)\] where \(c_i\) are real numbers and \(f(n)\) is a function of \(n\).

title: Counting with Reccursion
text:
More Definitions
\[a_n=c_1\cdot a_{n-1}+c_2\cdot a_{n-2} \cdots + c_k\cdot a_{n-k} +f(n)\]
If \(f(n)=0\) the recurrence is called homogeneous and if \(f(n) \ne0\) the recurrence is called non-homogeneous. All the examples on the previous slide are linear, but the Fibbonacci sequence is the only homogenous linear example on the last slide.
If a recurrence is not linear, the it is called a non-linear recurrence relation. An example of a non-linear recurrence is \(a_n=a_{n-1}\cdot a_{n-3}\).

Consider making \(k\) choices from a list of \(n\) possible choices. How many ways are there to do this?

Order matters and repetition is allowed: \(n^k\)

Order does not matter and repetition is not allowed: \(\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!k!}\)

The order of a recursive formula is the number of preceding values that are needed to calculate the next value. For example, the Fibonnacci recursion has order 2, and the Triangular number recursion has order 1.

Addition Principle
Idea: Break larger counting problem up into smaller and simpler counting problems then add up the results from the smaller problems.



Addition Principle
Suppose a set \(S\) is the disjoint union of smaller sets \(A_1, A_2, \cdots A_n\). That is \(S= A_1\cup A_2\cup \cdots A_n\) and \(A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset\) for \(i \neq j\). Then \(|S|=|A_1|+ |A_2| + \cdots + |A_n|\).

Idea: Create a step by step process to construct the object you are trying to count, and use the number of choices at each step to calculate the total number of different objects you can construct.
Multiplication Principle Consider a \(k\)-stage process that uniquely constructs all the elements of a set S. If \(\alpha_i\) is the number of choices at stage \(i\), then the number of elements in S is \(|S|=\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2 \cdots \alpha_k\).

The simplest and most common form of mathematical induction proves that a statement involving a natural number n holds for all values of n. The proof consists of two steps:

Base Case: showing that the statement holds when n is equal to the lowest value that n is given in the question. Usually, \(n = 0\) or \(n = 1\).
Inductive Step: showing that if the statement holds for some n, then the statement also holds when n + 1 is substituted for n.

We uses this proof technique to show infinitely manner statements are true.

title: Counting Tools
text:
Order and Repetition
Consider making \(k\) choices from a list of \(n\) possible choices. How many ways are there to do this?
In order to be able to answer this question we need to establish some rules, and we do this by answering two questions:
1. Does the order of our choices matter?
2. Are choices allowed to be repeated?

title: Counting Tools
text:
Order and Repetition
Order matters and repetition is allowed: \(n^k\)
Order matters and repetition is not allowed: \(n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-k+1)=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\)
Order does not matter and repetition is not allowed: \(\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!k!}\)
Order does not matter and repetition is allowed: To be determined.

title: Counting Tools
text:
Addition Principle
Idea: Break larger counting problem up into smaller and simpler counting problems then add up the results from the smaller problems.
Addition Principle Suppose a set \(S\) is the disjoint union of smaller sets \(A_1, A_2, \cdots A_n\). That is \(S= A_1\cup A_2\cup \cdots A_n\) and \(A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset\) for \(i \neq j\). Then \(|S|=|A_1|+ |A_2| + \cdots + |A_n|\).
The challenge and creativity of using this tool lies in choosing the right \(A_i\) sets.

title: Counting Tools
text:
Multiplication Principle
Idea: Create a step by step process to construct the object you are trying to count, and use the number of choices at each step to calculate the total number of different objects you can construct.
Multiplication Principle
Consider a \(k\)-stage process that uniquely constructs all the elements of a set S. If \(\alpha_i\) is the number of choices at stage \(i\), then the number of elements in S is \(|S|=\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2 \cdots \alpha_k\).
The challenge and creativity of using this tool lies in choosing the correct process, making sure it constructs all the objects you want to count, and does so uniquely..

title: Direct Proofs
text:
What is a Direct proof?
The simplest ,from a logic perspective, style of proof is a direct proof. Often all that is required to prove something is a systematic explanation of what everything means. Direct proofs are especially useful when proving implications. The general format to prove that statement P implies statement Q is: Assume statement P is true. Explain, explain, …, explain. Therefore statement Q is true. In this course there are two sorts of flavors of direct proof, “wordy” and “equation-y”.

title: Direct Proofs
text:
“Equation-y” Direct Proof Example
Here is a “equation-y” or symbolic manipulation direct proof of Pascal’s Triangle Identity. Claim: \(\binom{n}{k}+\binom{n}{k-1}=\binom{n+1}{k}\) Proof: \[\begin{eqnarray}
\binom{n}{k}+\binom{n}{k-1}
&=& \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}+\frac{n!}{(k-1)!((n-(k-1)!}\\
&=& \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}+\frac{n!}{(k-1)!((n+1-k)!}\\
&=& \frac{n+1-k}{n+1-k} \cdot \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}+\frac{k}{k} \cdot\frac{n!}{(k-1)!(n+1-k)!}\\
&=&  \frac{(n+1-k)n!}{k!(n+1-k)!}+\frac{k\cdot n!}{k!(n+1-k)!}\\
&=&  \frac{(n+1)n!-k\cdot n!+k\cdot n!}{k!(n+1-k)!}\\
&=& \frac{(n+1)!}{k!(n+1-k)!}\\
&=& \binom{n+1}{k} \square
\end{eqnarray}\]

title: Direct Proofs
text:
Second Direct Proof Example
Here is a bit of a mixture. Claim: If \(n\) is an even integer then \(n^2\) is even integer. Proof: Let \(n\) be an even integer. Then \(n=2k\) for some integer \(k\). Now \(n^2=(2k)^2=4k^2=2(2k^2)\) where \(2k^2\) is an integer. Hence \(n^2\) is even. \(\square\)

title: Direct Proofs
text:
“Wordy” Direct Proof Example
Here is a bit of a mixture. Claim:If \(n^2\) is an even integer then \(n\) is an even integer. Proof:
Let \(n\) be an integer. There are two cases for \(n\) it can be odd or even. If \(n\) is odd then \(n^2\) is odd. If \(n\) is even then \(n^2\) is even. The only case where \(n^2\) is even is the when \(n\) is even. \(\square\)
